newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says no evidence missing plane is stolen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says no evidence missing plane is stolen.

text.p: Defence officials said Wednesday they had no evidence of theft or sabotage in the disappearence last week of an A-10 warplane loaded with four bombs, and they are still trying to locate the plane.

"At this point we have no physical evidence that supports any of the theories out there being discussed," said a statement issued by Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Tucson, Arizona, which is coordinating the search for the plane.
"Our No. 1 objective is and always has been to find the pilot and the aircraft," it said. "Only upon doing that will we be able to begin looking into why this happened."

A spokesman for the Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona said new data from FAA radar in Denver had led investigators to extend the search for the missing plane to a location about 15 miles southwest of Vail, Colorado.
He said reviews of the FAA radar tapes had revealed a track believed to be that of the missing aircraft. In addition, calls to a special hotline had helped investigators narrow the search.

Kim Andree, spokeswoman for the Eagle County sheiff's office in Vail, said helicopters and fixed wing planes from the Civil Air Patrol searched the area on Wednesday, but bad weather hampered their efforts.

She said the rescue operation is focused on an area known as the New York Range where both the FAA data and eyewitness reports indicate a crash may have occurred. Two people reported seeing the plane and several others reported hearing a large sound around the time investigators believe a crash may have occurred. There were also reports of smoke, she said.

Washington officials said they were checking the pilot's background to see if it would provide any clues on what happened to the plane. They said a U-2 spy plane was to make a second try Wednesday to find the plane, south of Vail.
The tank-attacking A-10 Thunderbolt piloted by Capt. Craig Button, 32, has been missing since April 2 when it left the Tucson base for a bomb exercise in southwest Arizona.

Defence officials said the plane, carrying four 500-pound conventional Mark 82 bombs, simply disappeared from the rear of the three-plane formation. They said witnesses thought they heard the plane near Vail and a radar track showed a plane going in that direction although they cannot be certain it was the missing A-10.

Defence Department spokesman Capt. Michael Doubleday, at a Pentagon briefing on Tuesday, also dismissed speculation the plane may have been stolen, although he said officials simply do not know yet what happened to it.

"I don't think anybody at this point has a good enough idea of what occurred with the aircraft to have come up with any kind of a theory as to what might have caused it to go missing," Doubleday said.

But he said he understood there had been fresh snow in Colorado since the plane disappeared and "there are cases where aircraft disappear in the winter and then turn up some time later, after the snows have melted."
